claims.text: Moderate Ti and/or V additions improve the strength–plasticity balance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Ti and/or V additions induce local lattice distortions.
The induced local lattice distortions hinder dislocation motion.
The induced local lattice distortions activate additional plastic-deformation mechanisms.
Ti and/or V additions may form fine, well-dispersed secondary phases.
Fine, well-dispersed secondary phases act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The proposed structural changes promote favorable deformation mechanisms such as twinning.
Increased resistance to dislocation glide raises alloy strength.
Deformation twinning or other dislocation activities induced by Ti/V enhance ductility or plasticity.
The Ti/V-alloyed refractory HEA will have higher yield strength than an otherwise comparable refractory HEA without Ti/V additions.
The Ti/V-alloyed refractory HEA will have greater uniform elongation than the baseline alloy.
Under optimized processing, both yield strength and plastic strain are anticipated to improve by more than 10% relative to the baseline.
The beneficial effect holds under standard thermomechanical processing when the modified and baseline alloys are processed at the same temperature and cooling rate.
The alloy composition must be tuned to avoid excessive second-phase formation.
Excessive Ti/V additions may cause deleterious second-phase formation or embrittlement.
The improvement is sensitive to processing route and exact alloy composition.
